abstract: |
  We study the effects of training on racial disparities in the enforcement behavior of early-career Texas Highway Patrol officers. Exploiting the staggered timing of mandated in-service trainings, we find that race-focused trainings increase the White share of stops by 1.7 percentage points, whereas trainings focused on enforcement procedures have no impact on racial disparities. Changes in stop composition are driven by increased enforcement of White motorists and are consistent with a 30 percent decline in discrimination as measured by a “veil-of-darkness” test. Impacts of a cultural diversity training emphasizing racial stereotyping are particularly pronounced, highlighting the importance of curriculum details.
